questions.q: What is the author's central claim about genius?
options: Great work needs a disinterested obsession with something that matters
Great work comes from following promising paths
Natural ability is the one ingredient that really matters
Hard work alone produces great discoveries
questions.explain: He says the recipe for genius is a disinterested obsession with something that matters.

questions.q: Which pair of examples does the author give as people with obsessive interest in their subject?
options: Darwin and Ramanujan
Hamming and Trollope
Tolkien and Carlyle
Newton and Pasteur
questions.explain: He cites Darwin's interest in natural history and Ramanujan working out series on his slate.

questions.q: What did Newton's other two obsessions turn out to be, besides math describing the world?
options: Poetry and politics
Optics and astronomy
Alchemy and theology
Chemistry and medicine
questions.explain: Newton's alchemy and theology seem to have been complete wastes of time.

questions.q: How does the author teach his own kids?
options: He encourages them to go deep into whatever interests them
He drills them daily on the most important problems in each field
He has them start broad and delay specializing until college
He keeps their schoolwork and home projects on identical topics
questions.explain: He lets school handle the broad, shallow part and encourages them to go preposterously deep.

questions.q: Why might people do less great work after having children, according to the author?
options: Their natural ability declines once they become parents
A strong competing interest means they don't want to
They lack the energy that great work demands after having kids
Their ambition fades once they have a family to support
questions.explain: He says the real change is that interest competes with another powerful interest and you don't want to.
